title: I Took the Community Firewood-Split Hours to the Neighbor Who Camped the Block

parts.text: I walked to the splitter at 8:08 a.m. and neighbor Cal was already stacking on our numbered block. The sign said: ONE SPLITTER. FORTY MINUTES. WOOD STAYS WITH THE SLOT. I was fifty-one, co-op member, holding a tag that listed our cord. Cal shrugged. "Neighbors are the pile." I photographed the sign, the tag, and his maul on our block. Then I asked for the split log. At 8:16 the yard pinged why Cal's name was on our forty. I kept my voice yard-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A sign is only a sign until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The yard can see Cal's maul on our block during our slot.

social.video_title: He stacked on our numbered block in our forty — Part 1/2
social.description: Firewood yard, a neighbor on our block, a forty-minute sign he posted. I logged the maul. Would you have asked for the split log?

parts.text: Cal called it a wedge until the yard asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the sign, and the maul still. The block went back to our tag. Cal ran his own forty and told the next neighbor atmosphere was always about heat. Heat is a word neighbors use when a slot exists. Splitter policy now has a second line: NEIGHBORS ARE NOT THE PILE. I keep our tag on a labeled clip. Cal brown-bags his jokes. The yard finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Neighbors are not the pile — Part 2/2
social.description: Split log, numbered block, and a second line on the sign. Was a wedge ever our forty?
